'''''Dovyalis caffra''''',{{Efn|Until recently ''D. caffra''}}  commonly known as the '''Kei apple''',<ref>{{cite book|last=Sturtevant|first=Edward|title=Sturtevant's notes on edible plants|year=1919|url=https://archive.org/details/sturtevantsnotes00sturuoft|publisher=J.B. Lyon company, State printers|location=Albany|page=[https://archive.org/details/sturtevantsnotes00sturuoft/page/17 17]|isbn=978-0-486-20459-8 }}</ref> is a small to medium-sized tree, native to southern [[Africa]]. Its distribution extends from the [[Kei River]] in the south, from which the common name derives, northwards along the eastern side of the continent to [[Tanzania]]. The ripe fruits (which are present from December to January) are edible and similar in appearance to [[apricot]]s, though they are quite acidic due to having a high concentration of [[malic acid]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Taher |first1=Mohamed A. |last2=Tadros |first2=Louis K. |last3=Dawood |first3=Dawood H. |date=November 2018 |title=Phytochemical constituents, antioxidant activity and safety evaluation of Kei-apple fruit ( Dovyalis caffra ) |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0308814618309099 |journal=Food Chemistry |language=en |volume=265 |pages=144–151 |doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2018.05.099|pmid=29884365 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Dovyalis caffra in Global Plants on JSTOR |url=https://plants.jstor.org/compilation/dovyalis.caffra |access-date=2025-01-17 |website=plants.jstor.org}}</ref>

It is a usually found in dry types of woodland when it grows to 6 m tall. In moister types of open woodland it reaches its greatest size of about 8–9 metres. A tree, with sharp, 3–6 cm long stem spines in the leaf [[axil]]s, and large sturdy thorns. Buds at the base of the spine produce clusters of alternately arranged simple ovate [[leaf|leaves]] 3–6 cm long.

The [[flower]]s are inconspicuous, solitary or clustered, with no petals. It is [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], with male and female flowers on separate plants, though some female plants are [[parthenogenesis|parthenogenetic]].

The [[fruit]] is an edible bright yellow or orange globose [[Berry (botany)|berry]] 2.5–4 cm diameter, with the skin and flesh of a uniform colour and containing several small [[seed]]s. Production is often copious, weighing down the branches during the summer. They are juicy and very [[acid]]ic.

==Cultivation and uses==
A traditional food plant in the areas it occurs, this little-known fruit is considered by local efforts to improve nutrition, boost food security, foster rural development and support sustainable landcare.<ref>{{cite book |author=National Research Council |title=Lost Crops of Africa: Volume III: Fruits |url=http://books.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=11879 |access-date=17 July 2008 |volume=3 |date=25 January 2008 |publisher=National Academies Press |isbn=978-0-309-10596-5 |chapter=Kei Apple |chapter-url=http://books.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=11879&page=103 |archive-date=31 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120331010449/http://books.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=11879 |url-status=live }} [https://pdf.usaid.gov/pdf_docs/Pnads877.pdf Downloadable PDF] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210512170531/https://pdf.usaid.gov/pdf_docs/Pnads877.pdf |date=12 May 2021 }}</ref>

Kei-apples are often eaten fresh or sprinkled with [[sugar]] to complement their natural acidity. Aside from being eaten fresh, the fruit can be made into [[jam]], used in desserts, or [[pickling|pickled]] (their natural acidity means vinegar is not needed). In Kenya, it is mostly used for live fences and hedges.

Although it is native to southern Africa, it has also been introduced to the [[Mediterranean]], [[California]], [[Florida]], and other regions with [[subtropical]] and warm temperate climates. In these places it is most often grown as an [[ornamental plant]], being popular as an impenetrable [[hedge (gardening)|hedge]]. It is [[sodium chloride|salt]] and [[drought]]-tolerant, so useful for [[coast]]al landscaping in dry regions.

Although a subtropical species, the Kei apple is able to survive temperatures as low as {{Convert|-6|C}}. Gardeners who want fruit require a female plant; a fertile female plant and a fertile male plant is ideal. Kei apples are propagated by seed. Plants will bear about four years later.

== Taxonomy ==
The original species name ''caffra'' is related to [[Kaffir (racial term)|kaffir]], an ethnic slur used towards black people in Africa. At the July 2024 [[International Botanical Congress]], a vote was held with the result that "''caffra''" related names will be emended to ''afra'' related ones, with the implementation of this happening by the end of July 2024.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=McKie |first1=Robin |date=20 July 2024 |title=Botanists vote to remove racist reference from plants' scientific names |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/article/2024/jul/20/botanists-remove-racist-references-plants-scientific-names |access-date=21 July 2024 |work=The Observer |language=en-GB |issn=0029-7712}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
The species is invasive in New Caledonia.<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers12-08/010052239.pdf|title=Les espèces exotiques envahissantes de Nouvelle-Calédonie|last=Hequet|first=Vanessa|year=2009|page=17|language=fr|access-date=9 March 2019|archive-date=26 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191126160116/http://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers12-08/010052239.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>
